passage:
Imran: Api, the hostel fine came. I missed the mess bill deadline. Again.
Bhavna: Oh no. How much?
Imran: Not much. But it's everything. My notes are in six different notebooks. I can't sleep before 3. Then I miss the 9 am class.
Imran: At home Ammi reminded me of everything. School had bells. Here, nothing.
Bhavna: That sounds really overwhelming. You're not stupid, you know that?
Imran: Feels like it
Bhavna: Two things. One: this weekend we set up phone reminders for every bill and one notebook per subject. I'll do it on video with you.
Bhavna: Two: your college has a student wellness centre. Maybe talk to a counsellor there about the focus and sleep stuff. They can tell you if an evaluation would help.
Imran: That's not weird?
Bhavna: Not weird. Smart.
Imran: ok. Saturday?
Bhavna: Saturday.

qa.q: What does Imran miss after not sleeping before 3?
qa.a: The 9 am class.

qa.q: How is Imran feeling about hostel life, and what shows it?
qa.a: Imran feels overwhelmed and a bit stupid, with a missed bill, notes in six notebooks and sleepless nights.

qa.q: What choices does Bhavna offer, and why are they helpful?
qa.a: Setting up bill reminders and one notebook per subject together, and talking to a counsellor at the wellness centre who can say if an evaluation would help; that adds structure and proper support.

qa.q: How might Bhavna feel hearing 'Feels like it'?
qa.a: Bhavna may feel worried and protective, which is why Bhavna answered with practical help and called seeking support smart.

grounding: Shows a young adult overwhelmed by hostel life without the structure of home and school, and a sibling suggesting routines and a counsellor who can advise on an evaluation.

passage:
Vandana had been the top student in her village school, with Amma waking her at five and teachers checking every notebook. Now, three months into college in the district town, her hostel cupboard was a heap of loose pages. She had missed the exam form deadline by a day and paid the late fine from her food money. At night she lay awake, mind jumping from song to song.
Farhan, from her class, found her crying in the reading room. 'You're the sharpest one in our batch,' he said. 'What's going on?'
'I can't hold anything together without someone reminding me.'
He helped her buy a cheap wall planner and a file with coloured tabs. Then he said, 'The college has a visiting counsellor on Wednesdays. Might be worth asking about the sleep and focus. My cousin went. It helped.'
On Wednesday, Vandana went.

qa.q: What did Vandana pay the late fine from?
qa.a: Her food money.

qa.q: What does Vandana mean by 'I can't hold anything together without someone reminding me'?
qa.a: She means that without Amma and teachers structuring things, she feels lost and overwhelmed managing on her own.

qa.q: What choices helped Vandana start to cope?
qa.a: Using a wall planner and a tabbed file, and going to the visiting counsellor on Wednesday about sleep and focus.

qa.q: How might Farhan feel when he sees Vandana go to the counsellor?
qa.a: Farhan may feel glad the suggestion helped and relieved that his classmate is getting support.

grounding: Shows a young adult who was held together by home and school, overwhelmed at college, building routines and seeking support from a counsellor.

passage: First year at college in Bengaluru nearly broke me. At home, my mother had quietly held everything together: bills paid, alarms set, clothes washed. In the hostel nobody did. I'm Tejas, nineteen, and by October I had missed the mess-fee deadline twice, lost half my notes across three notebooks, and was lying awake at three in the morning with my mind racing. My roommate Varun found me surrounded by unpaid bills and said, "You're not stupid. You're just drowning." He helped me set phone reminders for every due date and one notebook per subject. Then he walked me to the student wellness centre, where a counsellor listened for an hour and suggested an assessment. Things aren't fixed. But I'm not drowning.

qa.q: How many times did Tejas miss the mess-fee deadline?
qa.a: Twice.

qa.q: How was Tejas feeling by October?
qa.a: Tejas felt overwhelmed and restless, lying awake with a racing mind.

qa.q: What steps helped Tejas start to cope?
qa.a: Phone reminders for due dates, one notebook per subject and visiting the wellness centre, where an assessment was suggested.

qa.q: How might Varun have felt finding Tejas among the unpaid bills?
qa.a: Varun was likely concerned and kind, choosing to help rather than mock.

grounding: Shows a young adult overwhelmed by hostel life without family scaffolding, building routines and seeking evaluation and support.

passage:
Warden's note, Room 12. Sudha, first year, has had a hard term. Her mess fees are two months overdue, not for lack of money but because she keeps forgetting; she showed me the unopened reminders in her bag. Her notes are spread across loose sheets, and she is often awake pacing the corridor at two in the morning. She cried when I asked, and said, "At home my father did all this. I didn't know how much." I didn't scold. We made a simple wall calendar together for fees and exams, and I walked her to the counselling cell, where they will arrange an evaluation. Next step: a Sunday check-in with me for the next month.
Rukmini

qa.q: How long are Sudha's mess fees overdue?
qa.a: Two months.

qa.q: How was Sudha feeling when the warden asked?
qa.a: She was overwhelmed and upset, crying about how much her father used to handle.

qa.q: What did Rukmini do to help Sudha?
qa.a: Made a wall calendar with her, walked her to the counselling cell for an evaluation and set up Sunday check-ins.

qa.q: How might Sudha's father feel if he knew?
qa.a: He might feel surprised and concerned, realising how much he had been holding together.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult overwhelmed by hostel life after years of family structure, helped with routines and an evaluation.

passage:
Sunday, 2 a.m. Can't sleep again. The phone bill was due Friday; I found the message today. My lab notes are in four different places, one of them apparently my brother Vaibhav's old backpack, which I brought to college by mistake. At school, Papa checked my timetable every night and Mummy packed my bag. I thought I was organised. Turns out they were. Today Vaibhav called, heard me crying, and didn't laugh. He said, "Set one alarm for every bill. And go to the counselling centre on Monday. Ask them about getting checked properly, so you know what's going on." I wrote both things on my hand so I won't forget. I'll go at ten.
Bhavna

qa.q: Where did Bhavna find some of the lab notes?
qa.a: In Vaibhav's old backpack.

qa.q: How is Bhavna feeling at 2 a.m.?
qa.a: Bhavna feels overwhelmed and restless, unable to sleep and upset about the missed bill.

qa.q: What steps did Vaibhav suggest?
qa.a: One alarm for every bill and going to the counselling centre to ask about a proper assessment.

qa.q: How did Vaibhav react when he heard Bhavna crying?
qa.a: He didn't laugh; he was kind and practical.

grounding: Shows a young adult realising parents had held things together, and turning to routines and an evaluation for support.

passage:
Elizabeth: Indu, the hostel office just fined me for missing the mess fee date. Again.
Indu: Oh no. Wasn't it on your list?
Elizabeth: I have five lists. On five different pieces of paper. Lost four.
Elizabeth: Also my notes for all three subjects are on my phone, laptop, and backs of receipts.
Indu: At home Amma and school kind of ran your whole schedule, right?
Elizabeth: Exactly. Now nobody does, and I'm drowning. I lie awake at 3 am thinking about everything I forgot.
Indu: That sounds exhausting. Want to set one phone reminder for every fee date tonight? I'll sit on call.
Elizabeth: Okay.
Indu: And maybe talk to the student counselling centre? They can help you figure out if an assessment makes sense.
Elizabeth: Scary but yeah. Booking it tomorrow at 10.
Indu: Proud of you 🤍

qa.q: Where does Elizabeth say the notes for all three subjects are kept?
qa.a: On the phone, the laptop, and the backs of receipts.

qa.q: What was Elizabeth feeling when writing about lying awake at 3 am?
qa.a: Elizabeth felt overwhelmed and anxious, drowning without the structure that home and school used to give.

qa.q: What two steps did Indu suggest, and why do they help?
qa.a: A phone reminder for every fee date adds a routine, and the counselling centre can help Elizabeth decide about an assessment and get proper support.

qa.q: How does Indu seem to see Elizabeth's struggle?
qa.a: Indu sees it as a real difficulty, not laziness, and feels caring and proud when Elizabeth decides to book help.

grounding: Elizabeth, no longer held together by home and school, is overwhelmed at the hostel and starts building routines and seeking assessment and support.
